chunks: From him, from his father, from Ubaydullah ibn Yahya, from a man, from Abd al-Hamid ibn Ghawwas al-Ta'i, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

My grandfather used to say: 'Hasten in supplication, for when a servant is one who supplicates frequently and an affliction befalls him and he supplicates, it is said (by the Angels): A well-known voice. And when he is not one who supplicates frequently and an affliction befalls him and he supplicates, it is said: Where were you before today?'

key_terms.الْبَلَاء: Affliction/trial — used in Islamic tradition for divinely-permitted hardship
key_terms.تَقَدَّمُوا: Hasten/precede — imperative form urging the audience to act before the need arises
key_terms.دَعَّاء: One who supplicates frequently — intensive form indicating habitual supplication
key_terms.صَوْتٌ مَعْرُوف: A well-known voice — implying the Angels recognize the supplicant

ai.seo_question: Why should one supplicate before times of hardship according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) transmits from his grandfather — understood to be Imam Ali ibn al-Husayn (Zayn al-Abidin, AS) or possibly Imam al-Baqir (AS) — the exhortation to make supplication a regular practice before times of hardship arrive. The hadith uses the vivid image of Angels recognizing the voice of a devoted supplicant as 'well-known,' while the prayer of someone who only calls in crisis is met with a rebuke. This teaching reflects the Shia emphasis on du'a as a continuous, anticipatory relationship with God rather than a merely reactive practice.
